     Filing1 (including all resource reports, tables, plans, alignment sheets, maps, deviations, and
     appendices) that have been updated to clearly indicate deleted and new text in a consistent
     format such as single strikethrough and replacement text as highlighted in yellow. For maps
     and alignment sheets, highlight all changes by drawing a wide, brightly colored outline
     (bubble) around the modified areas in the aerial imagery section only. Provide a separate
     table, listing the documents filed in the initial application2 on June 26, 2026 that were not
     revised in the supplemental filing.

modifications are located and are provided in Attachment 1 to this response. Gulf South notes that

wetland delineation report and addendum Phase I cultural resources survey report), 2) entirely

Response:


     a. Gulf South continues to coordinate with the respective landowners of the “Areas Not
        Surveyed” that are depicted on pages 96, 259, 343, and 344 of 398 to obtain the necessary
        survey permissions. The landowner of the “Areas Not Surveyed” that are depicted on

        survey area have been adjusted so that surveys are no longer required for the areas

     b. The areas illustrated as “Supplemental Environmental Survey Areas” on pages 231

      were made to the Project since the June 2026 Filing:

         tables and text, and correctly illustrated/labeled on the alignment sheets and maps.

      g. Per table 1 – Summary of Modifications to the Proposed Project, provided as part of
         the Supplemental Filing Narrative, multiple adjustments were made to avoid
         waterbodies, but the total waterbody count crossed by the Project increased by 6. Please

         Supplemental Filing Narrative, multiple adjustments were made to avoid impacts to
         wetlands, but the total wetland impact acreage increased. Please explain this
         discrepancy.

      table that was previously submitted as part of the Supplemental Filing (Accession Number

      response.

   b. The area located south of CR 1030 was originally surveyed in December 2025 and then
      re-surveyed in May 2026 due to the proposed route shift that was adopted as part of
      Modification 012. Wetland delineation data collected during the May 2026 survey, which
      coincided with the growing season, indicated that WS2015_PEM should be reduced in size
      based on the conditions documented at that time. As such, the alignment sheets provided
      in the Supplemental Filing (Accession Number 20260928-5070) accurately depict the

   c. As indicated in the revised resource report tables and exhibits provided as part of the
      Supplemental Filing (Accession Number 20260928-5070), HDD-07 was removed from the
      overall Project scope as part of Modification 024. Gulf South determined that HDD-07

      and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers property crossing with a conventional bore.

   d. TAR-105 is located on page 130 of the revised alignment sheets that were provided as part
      of the Supplemental Filing (Accession Number 20260928-5070). As such, the Summary of
      Modifications to the Proposed Project table has been revised accordingly and is provided
      as Attachment 2 of this response.

   e. To date, biological and cultural resource surveys have not been completed for TAR-052 as
      Gulf South continues to coordinate with the landowner to obtain the necessary survey
      permissions.

   f. As identified in the revised Table 8.2-2 and exhibits that were provided as part of the
      Supplemental Filing (Accession Number 20260928-5070), Gulf South proposes to utilize a
      total of five contractor yards (CY-02, CY-03, CY-09, CY-08, and CY-06) during

Section 1.1            Project Description

       Gulf South is filing an Application for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity
with FERC for authorization to construct, own, operate, and maintain new greenfield facilities and
modified and/or expanded existing facilities. Specifically, Gulf South is proposing to construct a
new approximately 154-mile-long155-mile-long natural gas pipeline comprised of 36-inch- and
42-inch-diameter pipe segments (herein referred to as the Texas Gateway Pipeline), three new
delivery meter and regulator (M&R) stations, and other appurtenant facilities in east Texas and
southwest Louisiana.       Gulf South also proposes to construct a new 13,410 nominal
horsepower1 (hp) compressor station (herein referred to as the Cleveland Compressor Station
[CS]) along its existing Index 129 Legacy System in San Jacinto County, Texas. Further, Gulf
South proposes to expand its existing Carthage Junction CS and Magasco CS by installing
additional compressor units capable of adding an additional 39,260 nominal hp2 and
44,961 nominal hp3 at the respective stations and a new bi-directional check M&R station at the
Carthage Junction CS. Overall, the Project will allow Gulf South to transport approximately
1.8 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas from existing facilities in Carthage, Texas to delivery
points in southeast Texas and southwest Louisiana.

Section 1.3.6          Construction Schedule

       To meet market demand, Gulf South’s planned in-service date for Project facilities is as
early as December 2028.         Pending all necessary authorizations and permits, Gulf South
anticipates mobilization and construction to start as early as 3rd Quarter 20271st Quarter 2028.
This schedule is based on the Gulf South’s request for final approval by the FERC no later than

Section 1.6).

                                       1.0   INTRODUCTION

       In June 2006, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) published a final rule for
40 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 122 to include Amendments to the National Pollutant
Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Regulations for Stormwater Discharge Associated with
Oil and Gas Exploration, Production, Processing, or Treatment Operations or Transmission
Facilities. This rule modified the NPDES regulations to exempt certain stormwater discharges
from field activities or operations, including construction associated with oil and gas exploration,
production, processing, or treatment operations or transmission facilities. These discharges are
exempt from permitting requirements except in situations when the construction-related activities
result in the discharge of a hazardous substance or oil in “reportable” quantities, or in situations
when the discharge of a pollutant other than sediment contributes to a violation of an applicable
water quality standard.

       The rule also encouraged the application of best management practices (BMPs) for oil
and gas field activities and operations to minimize the discharge of pollutants in stormwater runoff
and to protect water quality both during and after construction activities. Installation of effective
BMPs will help protect surface water during storm events and assist in assuring that there is no
discharge of a reportable quantity (RQ) or violation of a water quality standard.

       The primary purpose of this Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) is to minimize
the impacts of construction activities on stormwater runoff. The plan includes descriptions of the
following:
                Covered activities;
                Best Management Practices;
                Maintenance and Inspection Procedures;
                Plan Modifications;
                Required Reports, Documents, and Record Keeping; and
                Certifications.

       A stand-alone Spill Prevention and Response Procedures Plan (SPRPP) has also been
developed, and is incorporated by reference into this SWPPP as Appendix A. All personnel
engaging in construction activities will follow this SWPPP.

2.3     RUNOFF COEFFICIENT OF SOILS

        The potential for soil erosion caused by water is a concern in the construction and
operation of the Project. During construction, some existing vegetation will be removed and some
soils will be temporarily destabilized, increasing the potential for erosion. Such erosion is strongly
related to the permeability of a soil and to the cohesion of the soil particles that comprise a soil.
Other soil properties that influence water erosion include soil texture, percent organic matter, soil
structure, and soil infiltration capacity. Soils containing high proportions of silt and very fine sand
are the most erodible types, whereas well drained and well graded gravels and gravel-sand
mixtures with little or no silt are the least erodible. Erosion is also influenced by the slope length
and gradient; the frequency, intensity, and duration of rainfall; and the amount of time bare soils
are exposed.

        The Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) ranks soil erodibility as slight, low,
moderate, or high. Appendix B indicates the erodibility of each of the soils crossed by the Project.

        All previously vegetated areas will be restored and revegetated following the completion
of Project activities. The restoration plan for this Project was developed in accordance with the
FERC Upland Erosion Control, Revegetation, and Maintenance Plan (Plan) and Wetland and
Waterbody Construction and Mitigation Procedures (Procedures) utilizing either species
recommended by the NRCS or those consistent with the adjacent undisturbed areas.                   No
increases in runoff coefficients are expected in areas that are revegetated following the
completion of construction.

2.5     POTENTIAL SOURCES OF CONTAMINATION FROM CONSTRUCTION

        Potential sources of pollutants associated with construction that could be discharged into
stormwater during construction may include:
              Vehicle and Equipment Fueling and Maintenance.                  Fueling and minor
               maintenance of vehicles and equipment are conducted on some construction sites.
               Leaks and spills of fuel, oil, and grease are possible sources of contamination.
              Material Handling/Loading and Unloading Areas. Material handling/loading
               and unloading activities are common on construction sites. Materials may be
               spilled, leaked, or lost during loading and unloading, and may collect in the soil or
               other surfaces and be carried away in stormwater. Machines used to unload
               materials also may be a source of stormwater pollution.
              Erosion. Erosion is caused when soil is exposed to water, wind, or ice. Erosion
               can be caused by removing vegetation, compacting or disturbing the soil, changing
               natural drainage patterns, and covering the ground with impermeable surfaces
               (buildings, pavement, or concrete), all of which are integral parts of construction
               projects. Erosion is a source of sediment in stormwater.

                            3.0   BEST MANAGEMENT PRACTICES

       BMPs are controls used to prevent, minimize, or control stormwater pollution.            The
following guidelines will be used in the selection, design, and implementation of BMPs:

              The construction-phase erosion and sediment controls will be designed to retain
               sediment onsite to the extent practicable and to ensure that no significant changes
               occur in the volume or characteristics of stormwater runoff to receiving waters.
              All control measures will be properly selected, installed, and maintained in
               accordance with the manufacturer’s specifications and good engineering
               practices.
              If sediment is conveyed beyond the construction site, controls will be used to
               minimize off-site impact.

              Litter, construction debris, and construction chemicals exposed to stormwater will
               be prevented from becoming a pollutant source for stormwater discharges.

3.1    EROSION AND SEDIMENT CONTROLS

       Erosion and sediment controls that will be implemented include the following:

          Erosion Controls (primary protection)

4.1    AREAS TO BE INSPECTED

       Inspections will include all areas of the Project disturbed by construction activities and
areas used for storage of materials. This includes, but is not limited to construction areas that
have not reached final stabilization, areas used for storage of materials that are exposed to
precipitation (prevents inspection at a warehouse site), staging areas, access roads, structural

the extent practicable.

       If part of the construction area has reached final stabilization, the site will be logged and
mapped as final. Inspections will be discontinued upon confirmation of final stabilization.

4.2    INSPECTION SCHEDULE

       Inspections of BMPs will be completed on a daily basis in active areas of construction. In
inactive construction areas, inspections will be completed every 7 days and within 24 hours of
0.5-inch of rain or greater. Inspections will be performed until stabilization is achieved in all
disturbed areas.

4.3    DISTURBED AREAS

       EI(s) will inspect storage areas that are exposed to precipitation events, structural control
measures, and high-traffic areas. Sediment and erosion control measures will be inspected to
confirm that they are operating properly. Areas of entrance and egress for Project traffic will be
inspected for evidence of offsite sediment tracking. Inspections in disturbed areas will be in
accordance with FERC’s Plan and Procedures.

        The purpose of an HDD Plan is to identify operational procedures and responsibilities for
the prevention, containment, and clean-up of drilling fluids that have ponded on the ground
surface or within a waterbody during HDD operations. This HDD Plan defines methodologies to
control and minimize the impacts on sensitive resources from inadvertent returns of drilling fluids
associated with the proposed HDDs. The objectives of this HDD Plan are to:

            Minimize the potential for an inadvertent drilling fluid returns (IR) event;
            Enable the timely detection of an IR event;
            Provide for environmental protection of wetlands, waterbodies, and other sensitive
             resources, in the event an IR occurs;
            Establish response procedures to address containment and clean-up of an IR event;
             and
            Establish notification protocols with the applicable parties and regulatory agencies in
             the event an IR occurs.

        While drilling parameters will be established to maximize circulation and minimize risk of
IRs, the possibility of lost circulation and releases cannot be eliminated. Therefore, the following
plan has been prepared to document Gulf South’s procedures in the event of an IR. Gulf South’s

       The CMT and EMT have overall responsibility for implementing this HDD Plan and have

responsibility of all personnel on this Project, including the Contractor. Shared responsibilities

          Verify that all workers are properly trained and familiar with the implementation of the
           HDD Plan, prior to and during drilling operations.
          Monitor drilling fluid circulation back to the entry and exit locations.
          Maintain ongoing communication with the CMT, EMT, and Contractor personnel when
           a suspected IR occurs.
          Stop or change the drilling program in the event of an observed or anticipated IR.
          Verify that all drilling equipment is in working order, including annular pressure
           monitoring equipment.
          Monitor the HDD alignment for IRs and other signs of environmental impacts.
          Ensure the proper site personnel are informed of an IR; coordinate personnel,
           response, clean-up, regulatory agency notification; and verify all waste materials are

                                 10.0 CONTINGENCY PLAN

          If the corrective actions described above do not correct the problem, Gulf South may opt
to abandon the drill hole and consider alternate measures. Abandonment procedures and
alternative measures will be discussed with appropriate permitting and regulatory agencies and
approvals secured. Abandonment procedures and alternative crossings are described in the
subsequent sub-sections.

          Generally, there are four times for failure during the HDD process: the pilot hole
installation, hole opening or expansion, the pullback processes, or an overriding mechanical
failure. Initiating the pilot hole is the first step in the HDD process, which is drilled along a
predetermined path. Drilling fluid is released when drilling to assist with cutting the soil or rock
strata, lubricating the drill stem, removing drilled cuttings and forming a wall cake to reinforce the



                                                    23
 TEXAS GATEWAY PROJECT                                                                         HDD PLAN



structural integrity of the hole. Failure during the pilot hole process will occur if the hole collapses
during the drilling process. This may be due to unfavorable stratum containing non-cohesive
alluvial soil or loose gravel, or by not forming a solid wall cake to keep the hole stable. The HDD
installation method will be considered a failure if there are two unsuccessful attempts at
completing a pilot hole. With a stuck drill stem, attempts must be made to retrieve it. Utilizing
torque and tension from the drill rig, the drill pipe may be removed.              If all attempts are
unsuccessful, abandonment of that hole will occur and alternative crossing methods such as
selection of an alternate drill path may be appropriate.

       The second potential for failure occurs during the hole opening phase. This is a multi-step
process that may require a significant length of time. In this process, the hole opening tools are
attached to the string used to initiate the pilot hole. This tool is then pulled back towards the drill
rig from the pre-determined exit point while rotating. In order to obtain the necessary width for
the pipeline, this is done multiple times while increasing the hole opening tool's diameter. The
potential for failure during the hole opening process increases with the amount of time utilized to
drill the hole. Failure will occur if materials fall into the hole due to the lack of a good wall cake.
With each tool that passes and dispenses drilling fluid, caverns throughout the hole may form
leading to instability in the hole and causing the backup of the excavated materials in the drilled
hole. As the drill pipe passes, it will encounter increased friction from the backup of the excavated
materials causing the pipe to slow or stop rotating. If the hole opening tool breaks within the hole,
the hole opening pass can resume only if the parts can be retrieved. The HDD installation method
will be considered a failure if there is one unsuccessful attempt at opening the hole to the
necessary diameter. If tools or parts are lost while drilling, the Contractor will have seven days to
retrieve any missing parts in order to continue using the selected hole. If the parts are not
retrieved within seven days, abandonment of the hole will occur. In this case, a new drill path can
be utilized, or the drill path can be adjusted to avoid any problematic stratum. New drill paths will
need to be evaluated and approved by relevant regulatory agencies.

       The pullback process of the prefabricated pipeline into the drilled hole is the last step of
the HDD process. The pipe is led through the hole using a string attached to a swivel. The swivel
should keep the pipe from rotating while being passed through the hole. The pipe is also filled
with water to keep it neutrally buoyant with the collected drilling fluid already within the hole.
Without water, the pipe would float increasing the chance for resistance from the friction of the
contact on the ceiling which could damage the pipe itself. Failure may occur if the pipe becomes
lodged and cannot be moved in either direction. Unless the pipe can be removed from the hole,

10.1   ABANDONMENT

       In the event the drill hole is to be abandoned the following procedures will be implemented:

           chosen based on the geologic formations along the drilling hole.

           At the surface (within approximately 5 feet of the surface), Gulf South will fill the drill
           end points with compacted soil and grade the location to the original contour.

           If deemed necessary by Gulf South or the USACE, the Contractor may be required to
           complete more extensive grouting to reduce the risk of ground subsidence and/or
           returns of inadvertent drilling fluid from adjacent HDD alignments, to reduce the risk of
           seepage through the drill path, or to comply with applicable regulatory requirements
           or other Project conditions.

10.2   ALTERNATIVE CROSSINGS

       Before any determination of alternative crossings, an attempt will be made to identify and
assess the reason for the drill failure as this may be critical for selection of the alternate.
Consideration of alternatives will include but not be limited to:

          horizontal relocation of the drill hole;

        The nature of the Project may provide exposed topsoil for potential recruitment of noxious
weeds and invasive species, and the potential exists for equipment to transport noxious weed
and/or invasive species seeds/spores to areas without infestations. In order to counteract this
potential introduction, Gulf South Pipeline Company, LLC will implement standard control measures
that will be used to minimize the introduction and spread of noxious weed and invasive species
including:

                Follow the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Upland Erosion Control,
                 Revegetation, and Maintenance Plan and the Wetland and Waterbody Construction
                 and Mitigation Procedures to assure that sediment movement and the associated
                 movement of non-native seeds into newly disturbed soils are minimized.

                Use construction techniques within the Project workspace that minimize the time
                 that bare soil is exposed and, therefore, minimize the opportunity for exotic species
                 to become established.

                For waterbody and wetland construction, construction equipment and materials will
                 be restricted to what is necessary and all equipment and materials will be checked
                 prior to and following use for any vegetation or debris to be removed.

                In wetland construction areas where practicable, remove topsoil from the excavation
                 areas and store it to the side for replacement once construction is complete. This
                 will minimize the introduction of non-native species and maintain the native plant
                 seed bank.

                Sow a cover crop along all exposed soil surfaces as soon as practicable to assure
                 that a suitable growing substrate for noxious weed or invasive species is not
                 available for long periods of time.
